records.question: What is the current average coral cover in American Samoa according to the Executive Summary?
ground_truth_chunks: - Average coral cover is now 36%, higher than the averages for the Pacific, South Pacific, U.S. Pacific, Indian Ocean, Great Barrier Reef, and Caribbean. The latter two have just 10% and 8-18% coral cover left, respectively. Coral cover is lower than it was here before crown-of-thorns starfish ate almost all the coral in 1978, and lower than it was in the past in the Pacific, Indian Ocean and Caribbean.
- Coral cover has increased over the 8 years of this monitoring program, while coral cover has decreased in the Caribbean, Pacific, Indian Ocean, Red Sea, and Great Barrier Reef.

records.question: What range and mean of coral cover were reported across the 11 reef slope sites?
records.ground_truth_answer: Coral cover ranged between 13% and 59%, with a mean of 36%.
ground_truth_chunks: Benthic cover on each of the 11 sites is shown in Figure 2 below. There are large differences between sites. Coral cover is highest at Aunu'u, Fagamalo, Leone, Aoa, and Fagatele. It is lowest in Vatia, Amaua, and Faga'alu. Coral cover ranged between 13% and 59%, with a mean of 36%.

records.question: Between which years did coral cover at Aoa increase to a new higher level?
ground_truth_chunks: Coral cover did not show net change until between 2007 and 2008, at which an increase to a new higher level occurred.
Coral cover at Aoa is now quite high at over 50%, one of the highest of the sites in the monitoring program.

records.question: Which coral genus has the most cover in transects?
records.ground_truth_answer: Montipora has the most cover in transects.
ground_truth_chunks: Coral genera with the most cover in transects are shown in Figure 27. This pattern is similar to those in previous years. *Montipora* has the most cover, followed by *Porites*, *Acropora*, and *Pavona*, and other genera have less cover.

records.question: Which invertebrate was recorded as the most common in the 50 cm wide belt transects?
ground_truth_chunks: The orange sponge *Sylissa* sp. was the most common invertebrate, followed by the encrusting sponge *Dysdea* sp., groups of holes produced by an unknown species, the colonial ascidian *Atriolum robustum*, tiny hermit crabs in holes in corals, the small burrowing urchin *Echinostrephus* wp., the Christmas tree worm, *Spirobrachus gigantea*, and grooves in coral produced by alpheid (snapping) shrimp.

records.question: Between which years did coral cover at Gataivai experience the largest drop?
ground_truth_chunks: Coral cover shows a slight decreasing trend over the monitoring period, with the largest drop between 2011 and 2012.
The cause of this drop is not known, the transect tapes are placed close to the same location each year.

records.question: Which three coral genera had the most cover on both reef slopes and reef flats?
ground_truth_chunks: *Acropora* is the genus with the most cover on reef flats, followed by *Montipora*, *Porites*, *Pocillopora*, *Pavona* and *Isopora*.
On reef slopes, the genera with the most cover were *Montipora, Porites*, *Acropora*, *Pavona*, *Leptastrea* and *Pocillopora*, in that order, as shown in Figure 26.
*Montipora*, *Porites* and *Acropora* were the three genera with the most cover on both slopes and reef flats, but their order was different in the two zones.

records.section_heading: 1. The Introduced and Invasive Soft Coral, Carijoa riisei
records.question: Where and at approximately what depth did the DMWR diving team first observe Carijoa riisei in November 2012?
records.ground_truth_answer: In front of the cannery in the harbor, at about 50 feet deep.
ground_truth_chunks: About November, 2012, a DMWR diving team including the author surveyed an area in front of the cannery in the harbor where there will be a construction project. During the survey, Alice Lawrence took a couple pictures at about 50 feet deep of something she had not seen before. Later she showed them to the author, and it was clear that it was *Carijoa riisei*.

records.question: In April 2012, what specific signs of disease were observed on Acropora muricata staghorn in the Onososopo backreef pool?
records.ground_truth_answer: The staghorn was partly dead with white sections near the ends of some branches; often the branch tip remained alive with a white band about 5-10 cm long below it; sometimes part of the white area was light green indicating earlier death; the condition appears to be a disease and there was a sharp demarcation between diseased area near the mouth of the harbor and adjacent healthy area.
ground_truth_chunks: In April, 2012, an area of *Acropora muricata* staghorn in the Onososopo backreef pool was observed by the author to be partly dead, with white sections near the ends of some branches.
Often the branch tip remained alive, but a white band about 5-10 cm long was below it.
This appears to be a disease. There was a sharp demarcation between the area nearest the mouth of the harbor which had this disease, and the much larger area next to it that did not.

records.section_heading: Appendix III. Coral bleaching patterns among coral species
records.question: Which coral genera are reported as most vulnerable to bleaching and which genus is reported as less subject to bleaching?
records.ground_truth_answer: Acropora, Millepora, and Pocillopora are reported as most vulnerable to bleaching; Porites is reported as less subject to bleaching.
ground_truth_chunks: In general, they have reported that *Acropora*, *Millepora*, and *Pocillopora* are among the genera most vulnerable to bleaching. *Porites* is among the genera less subject to bleaching.
Branching species are generally more subject to bleaching than massives.
